To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

AICA ribosile is able to stimulate insulin release from pancreatic islets, and that this action is not associated with any significant change in the rate of glucose metabolism, the ATP content or the activity of the KATP channels.

AICA ribosides causes an insulinotropic action that is not associated with any significant changes in islet ATP content and that the effect of this nucleoside on insulin release is not due to an inhibition of the ATP-sensitive K+ channels in the plasma membrane of the pancreatic beta cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of AICA ribose and AICAR on insulin secretion.
the effects of AICA ribose on pancreatic islet function, with the aim of elucidating its mechanism(s) of action.
the insulinotropic effect of AICA ribotide, a compound which is known to inhibit the enzyme adenylate deaminase.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ZMP and/or ZDP, rather than ZTP, are the active metabolites of AICA ribose in the stimulation of pancreatic islet function.

AICA ribosides and its metabolites are able to stimulate insulin secretion from pancreatic islets by acting on a mechanism which is not dependent on the generation of ATP and the activation of ATP-sensitive K-channels.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ZMP, ZTP, and ZDP are potent stimulators of pancreatic beta cells, and that the effects of ZMP and ZTP are additive.
ZMP and ZTP are not the only nucleotides that can act as insulinotropic agents.
the effects of AICA ribonucleoside and its metabolites on insulin secretion are not due to a direct action on the glucose sensor of pancreatic beta-cells.
